sources_considered.why: The original September version directly studies coding hallucinations, but varies prompts rather than engineering-task complexity.
HCAST measures declining task success with increasing human completion time. It is earlier than the target period and does not measure a corresponding hallucination-rate trend.
Relevant contemporary evidence of difficult-task failures, but does not isolate the claimed increase in hallucinations.
Section 5.3 examines vulnerability risk among hallucinated samples, a different quantity from the probability of hallucinating.
The retrieved passages distinguish hallucination types and contextual coding difficulties but do not establish the required complexity gradient.

evidence_items.explanation: The study documents library hallucinations and sensitivity to prompt variations. It does not establish that increasing engineering-task complexity increases hallucinations; the retrieved record also does not specify exact experimental dates.

unresolved_gaps: No located evaluation jointly measures coding-task complexity, failure rates and hallucination rates under comparable conditions for the target period.
Lower benchmark success is insufficient to establish more hallucination.
The speaker supplies neither a complexity measure nor a definition of hallucination.
